units.text: Welcome. If you’ve ever looked at two AWS designs that both seem right and wondered which one to choose, you’re in the right place. This course is for people who know the AWS basics and want to think through the bigger decisions an architect faces.

We’ll start with what the business needs, draw the design, and compare what each option costs or protects. As you watch, pause at each decision and pick your answer before I explain mine. That’s good practice for the exam and for real architecture reviews. Let’s get started.
This is the AWS Certified Solutions Architect Professional visual course, SAP C zero three. Here’s what we will cover and how the course is organized.

Start with the card on the left. Multi-account and hybrid designs put several requirements in play at once. We will look at how security, recovery, cost, and the work of operating a system affect the same choice.

The middle card shows who this is for: architects, engineers, and experienced AWS practitioners. On the right is what to practice: choosing a design, then explaining why it fits better than a plausible alternative.
The strip at the bottom shows the method. Follow a real scenario through a diagram, compare the trade-offs, and use the result to answer an exam-style question.

Follow the trail from left to right. Cloud architecture and security, compliance, and governance account for twenty-five percent each of the scored exam. Think of those as two questions: how does the workload fit together, and who or what is allowed to cross its boundaries?

Cost-optimized architecture is fifteen percent. The resilience, migration, and business continuity domain is also fifteen percent. Ask which costs the design adds and what it takes to restore or move the workload.
Operational excellence and automation make up the remaining twenty percent. A design is only as useful as the team’s ability to operate it and verify that recovery works.
Use the sequence at the bottom: learn how it works, compare the options, then apply the decision. We will try that on a claims database.

Read the requirements on the right before looking at the database. Claims data must stay in one AWS Region. The application has a thirty-minute recovery target, requires private hybrid access, and should be simple to operate.

Follow the private connection from on premises into the approved Region. Here, an R D S Multi A Z D B instance replicates synchronously from the primary in A Z A to the standby in A Z B. The two Availability Zones are in the same Region.
The cross-Region replica is crossed out. It may serve a different recovery goal, but here it would take claims data out of the approved Region. A hard residency rule eliminates that option.

The scenario covers an Availability Zone failure, not a Region outage. The drill measured the application ready after eighteen minutes, against a target of thirty. That is a result from one test, not a guarantee. Measure when the application can do its job again, not just when the database switches over.

Now look at the whole claims portal. At the left, the edge serves static assets to international users. Follow the gold line instead for creates and updates. Those claims writes go to the approved Region. The edge artwork is not a database endpoint.

The dashed box marks where claims records and backups stay. The primary is in A Z A, the standby is in A Z B, and the backup remains inside the Region. The security callout rules out a cross-Region copy for this workload.

At the right, the operations test is a successful claim write after failover. Eighteen minutes was measured against a thirty-minute target. Below the Region box, the resilience note reminds us that a standby in another A Z does not fix a Region outage.
At the lower left, weigh ongoing standby cost against the cost of downtime. The cheapest option is only a candidate if it still meets residency and recovery requirements.
Start at the upper left. Trace the diagram from the client to the data store. Be able to say what each hop does, not just name the components.
Move clockwise to Compare. Identify what each option improves and what it costs or cannot do. In the claims example, better protection from a Region outage does not override residency.
At the lower right, solve the scenario. Choose the option that satisfies the hard requirements and name a test that would verify it.
Finish at the lower left. If your choice fails the test, follow the path again and identify the assumption you got wrong. That is how a diagram builds judgment you can transfer to the next problem.

The developer at the left deploys the reporting app. That does not make the developer the caller. Inside E C two, the instance profile associates the Report Reader role with the instance. The app uses temporary role credentials available through instance metadata.

Follow the green line to S three. The app calls Get Object for reports slash Q one dot C S V. To evaluate that request, identify the runtime principal, the action, the object, and any policy conditions that apply.

The evidence panel shows S T S Get Caller Identity run in the authorized app runtime with the same credentials. Assumed role, followed by Report Reader and the session name, identifies the role session. It tells us who made the call, not whether S three will authorize it.

The first panel shows an I A M user. It can have long-term access keys when needed. Unlike credentials that expire at the end of a session, long-term keys need active management. Do not make them the default for workloads.

In the middle, the role has a clock. When an authorized workload or federated user assumes a role, the session credentials are temporary. For the E C two app we just saw, the instance role avoids putting a permanent key into the application.

The crown at the right is the account root user. Protect it with multi-factor authentication and reserve it for tasks that actually require root. For routine access, use temporary credentials and scope the permissions to the work.

Read down the identity policy on Analyst Role. The effect is Allow. The action is S three Get Object. The resource scopes it to objects under blue in the exam reports bucket, and the condition requires an existing object tag of Project equals Blue.

Both reads use the same action and reach objects under the blue prefix. Q one has the Blue project tag, so this Allow matches. Q two is tagged Gold, so the condition fails. A prefix and a tag are separate checks.

The policy is attached to the role; it does not name a Principal field. A resource policy or role trust policy does name who it addresses. And an Allow that does not match is not an explicit Deny. You still have to evaluate the other applicable policies.
The top row fixes the request: an I A M role in a member account asks S three to delete an object from a bucket in its own account. The action stays the same as we compare the three policy outcomes.
On the left, the role policy allows the action, but an applicable service control policy explicitly denies it. The request is denied. Giving the role another Allow would not change that result.

In the middle, the service control policy permits the action, but there is no effective Allow, so the request is implicitly denied. On the right, an effective Allow exists and the applicable controls permit it. Diagnose a missing grant differently from a matching Deny.
Start in the caller account, on the left. The identity policy tells us what the role is permitted to request. In this example the role is requesting access to an S three bucket in another account.

Follow the cross-account arrow. The bucket policy on the right tells us which principals the resource owner authorizes. This direct cross-account request needs permission on both sides, with no applicable control blocking it.

The note below shows a different request: Assume Role. The target role's trust policy controls who may assume it. After authorized assumption, the new role session makes the later request under its own permissions. Distinguish access to a bucket from permission to assume a role.

The blue circle shows the actions an identity policy allows. The gold circle shows what the boundary permits. Their overlap is what this identity grant can provide. A boundary by itself never gives the identity permission.

Read the worked example across the bottom. The role policy allows S three read and delete, but the boundary permits only read. From that identity policy, only read survives. A delegated administrator cannot expand that identity grant by attaching a broader role policy.

The note below matters: evaluate any resource policy separately and check exactly which principal it names. The Venn diagram explains effective identity permissions, not every way a request can be authorized.

Follow the upper lane. The member account's role requests Get Object from an external bucket over T L S. Even though I A M and the bucket policy allow the read, the applicable service control policy denies it. The guardrail follows the member principal.

Now follow the lower lane. An external partner requests Put Object against the member account's bucket. I A M and the bucket policy allow it, but the example uses plain H T T P. The applicable resource control policy requires T L S, so the write is denied.

Ask which side is protected. A service control policy limits principals in member accounts. A resource control policy limits access to supported resources in member accounts, including by outside callers. Neither policy grants permission.

The reporting app assumes Report Role separately for each job. The role's identity policy allows S three read and Dynamo D B read. Each Assume Role request carries a session policy for just the resource access that particular job needs.

Read across the outcome table. The daily report's session can read from S three but not Dynamo D B. The table export has the opposite result. Narrowing one session does not change the underlying role or the other session.

The overlap is the role's identity permissions and the session policy. Since the role lacks S three write, the session policy cannot add it. The bottom note separates direct same-account resource grants to a session; this example is about identity permissions.
Cross-account access starts by asking which identity makes the final request. On the left, the Reporting App in Account A wants one approved report from Account B.
Follow Assume Role across the top to S T S. The application needs permission to assume Report Reader, and the role in Account B must trust the application’s principal.
S T S returns short-lived role credentials. The application then signs Get Object for reports slash q four dot c s v as the assumed role, not as its original identity.
Separate the two decisions. The trust policy governs who can assume the role. The role’s permissions and applicable guardrails govern what the session can do after assumption.
The monitoring vendor works for two customers. The external I D lets the receiving role verify which customer context the vendor is using, even though both requests come from the same vendor.
In the green path, Customer A’s external I D matches the condition on Customer A’s role. The role still trusts the vendor principal explicitly. Both checks matter.
Follow the red path. The request presents Customer B’s identifier to Customer A’s role. That trust condition does not match, so this request does not get a role session.
After a successful assumption, the role’s permissions still limit access to the approved report. The external I D is not a password and does not grant data access.
Role chaining changes which credentials are active. Start at the human session. The first Assume Role call checks the caller’s permission and Role A’s trust policy.
Now use Role A’s temporary credentials for the next Assume Role call. Check Role A’s permissions and Role B’s trust. The starting human credentials are not used for that second hop.
Follow the final arrow. The target API request uses Role B’s session credentials. The boxed limit is for that chained role session: at most one hour.
In an exam scenario, trace each trust decision in order, then evaluate the permissions of the identity that actually signs the final request.
Attribute-based access control can use a common policy across projects. Start with the operations role on the left, where the trusted Project value is Blue.
Read the policy in the middle. The String Equals condition compares the principal’s Project tag with the target instance’s Project tag for the Start Instances request.
On the right, Instance A is tagged Blue, so this allow applies. Instance B is tagged Gold. This statement does not allow the request to that instance.
Control who can supply or change these authorization tags. Then verify that the action supports the condition keys and check the rest of the policies before declaring a request allowed.
These two AWS workloads both use roles, but they do not use the same kind. Ask who assumes the role, then ask who controls its permissions.

Follow the upper lane. The Lambda function uses its execution role to write CloudWatch application logs. The trust names Lambda, and you scope the permissions to the APIs and resources the function needs.

The lower lane shows EC2 Auto Scaling. It uses a service-linked role for service-owned operations, such as launching instances. The service defines its permissions; do not treat it as an ordinary application role.
Choose a scoped execution role for custom function access. For Auto Scaling’s own service operations, use its service-linked role and respect the service-managed lifecycle.
There are two common ways to share an AWS resource across accounts. Decide whether the caller should assume an identity in the other account or use its existing identity against a shared resource.
On the left, Account A calls S T S to assume a role in Account B. Check the caller’s permission and the target role’s trust. Later resource calls use the new role session.
On the right, the caller keeps its Account A identity and reads from an Account B bucket. For this cross-account example, check the caller’s policy and the bucket’s resource policy.
Use role assumption for controlled access across resources or APIs. Use a resource policy for supported direct sharing, and evaluate applicable denies and service-specific conditions either way.
A data perimeter aligns three controls. It checks the identity making the request, the resource it targets, and the network path the request takes.
Follow the allowed request through each gate. The member-account principal reaches a resource in the trusted organization, and the request comes through an approved endpoint.
Compare the examples below. An external principal, a target bucket outside the organization, and an unapproved endpoint each fail a different gate.
Some requests made by AWS services do not carry the original network context. Design narrowly scoped exceptions for approved service calls and test the condition keys each service actually supports.
A V P C endpoint policy is an extra authorization filter. Start with the first panel, where a request passes through an endpoint to a supported service.
Now look at the middle panel. The endpoint policy cannot grant the needed identity permission or replace a resource policy. Evaluate every applicable policy for the caller and target.

On the right, use the endpoint policy to narrow which principals, actions, and resources may use that path. An applicable explicit deny still wins. Traffic on another path is not controlled by this endpoint policy.
Keep three checks separate: network reachability, the endpoint policy, and the service’s authorization decision. Passing one does not prove the others.
IAM Access Analyzer helps you find access outside a defined zone of trust. In the upper example, a bucket policy can allow an external principal to read an object.
Follow the policy to the analyzer. Its finding is evidence that access is possible under the policy, not proof that the external principal actually used that access.
Review the principal, resource, action, and conditions. If sharing is intended, document it. If it is unintended, narrow the policy and verify that the finding resolves.
Access Analyzer does not apply an automatic deny. Use CloudTrail for recorded API activity, and keep unused-access analysis and policy validation separate from external-access findings.
